三排弦豎琴起源於十六世紀義大利，為後文藝復興半音音樂，先加第二排五聲音階弦於第一: The triple-strung harp originated in sixteenth-century Italy, for the chromatic music of the late Renaissance: a second row of strings in a pentatonic scale was added beside the first diatonic row, and then a second diatonic row on the other side. Double and triple harps were common in Italy, Spain and France in the Baroque period, for solo playing and for basso continuo. It came to the British Isles early in the seventeenth century; in 1629 a French harpist brought a gut-strung triple harp to the court of Charles I, and London Welsh harpists quickly took it up, and by the early eighteenth century it was called the Welsh harp. Nineteenth-century accounts show that modulation required adjusting the outer rows, with the middle row supplying sharps and flats, which was solved only when the pedal harp appeared. After the twentieth century the pedal harp took over, followed by a revival of teaching and instrument making.
威爾士三弦豎琴琴體主要採用上等木材製作，通常選用櫻桃木、胡桃木或橡木打造琴身與共: The body of the Welsh triple harp is mainly of fine woods, usually cherry, walnut or oak for the body and soundbox, to keep the tone warm and resonant. The neck and support structure use hard oak or maple for stability. The strings were traditionally gut, while modern strings are often nylon or phosphor bronze. The pillar and the tuning mechanism are of brass or other metal, and some decoration may use ivory or bone.
威爾士三弦豎琴音色溫潤柔和，具有獨特的穿透力與歌唱性。其音質既明亮清晰，又不失溫: The Welsh triple harp has a warm, soft timbre with a distinctive carrying power and a singing quality. The tone is bright and clear yet warm and thick, and the range is wide, spanning three octaves. The instrument has three parallel rows of strings, which gives the timbre depth and layered resonance: the middle register is full and round, the top clear and bright, the bottom steady and strong. Its resonance is unusual: the three rows vibrate against one another and produce rich overtones, making a sound like a wind instrument and a keyboard instrument combined. Compared with the brilliance of the classical harp, the triple harp is more national in character, with something old and bleak; compared with the distant, ethereal harp, it is more concentrated and forceful, closer to the intimacy of the guitar and the zither.

威爾斯三排弦豎琴今日主要見於傳統威爾斯民間音樂，也曾在巴洛克時期用於獨奏與通奏低: Today the Welsh triple harp is heard mainly in traditional Welsh folk music, and in the Baroque period it was used for solo playing and continuo and entered the court. Modern occasions include folk bands, the triple-harp group Middle Row, busking, non-Welsh players and a few classical harpists; its repertoire is mostly art-music variations on Welsh tunes, and the composer Richard Barrett has also written for it.
The Welsh triple harp is a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 322.212.3, used mainly in traditional Welsh folk music. A beginner first learns the three-row layout: the outer row on the right-hand side is the bass row, the outer row on the left-hand side is the treble row, and the two outer rows are tuned alike and diatonically; the middle row supplies sharps and flats. To change key, particular notes on the outer rows must be adjusted, for example from C to G all Fs are raised a semitone; to F all Bs are lowered a semitone. For a passing sharp or flat the player inserts a finger between two outer strings and takes the note from the middle row. The harp can be held in the Welsh traditional way, on the left shoulder. Practice can begin with fast alternation of the same note between the two hands, making the doubled note of the outer rows.
威爾斯三排弦豎琴（telyn deires）屬弦鳴樂器，H-S編號322.212: The Welsh triple harp (telyn deires) is a chordophone, H-S number 322.212.3. It uses three parallel rows of strings instead of the usual single row: the two outer rows are tuned alike to the diatonic scale and the middle row supplies sharps and flats. The player divides the outer rows between the left and right hands and, where needed, puts a finger between the outer strings to take a semitone from the middle row; the two hands also often play the outer rows rapidly together, doubling the octave. It is now heard mostly in traditional Welsh folk music.
